need: Meet the four tests of statehood
what: The usual checklist comes from the 1933 Montevideo Convention, Article 1: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to deal with other States. Article 3 says a State exists regardless of whether others recognize it. In practice, a platform with rotating staff struggles on population, a site with no territory fails the second test, and capacity depends on other States being willing to talk. The International Court of Justice said in 2010 that declaring independence is not itself illegal, which leaves open whether the declaration achieves anything.

sources.t: Montevideo Convention 1933 (Yale Avalon Project)
ICJ, Kosovo advisory opinion 2010, full text (lagen.nu copy)

need: Have land the law lets you hold
what: Artificial islands have no territorial sea (UNCLOS Art. 60(8)). The high seas cannot be claimed (Art. 89), the deep seabed cannot be appropriated (Art. 137), Antarctica takes no new claims (Antarctic Treaty Art. IV), and space cannot be appropriated (Outer Space Treaty Art. II). The old route, occupation of land belonging to no one, is a method used by States, and the Court in Western Sahara held that lands lived on by organized peoples never qualified. Two strips of land are left in play, and each sits between neighbors with border guards.

sources.t: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, full text
Antarctic Treaty, text (Antarctic Treaty Secretariat)
Outer Space Treaty, text (UNOOSA)
ICJ, Western Sahara advisory opinion 1975, full text (lagen.nu copy)

what: UN Charter Article 4 opens membership to peace-loving States, by a General Assembly decision on a Security Council recommendation. The Council needs nine of 15 votes, including no veto from any of the five permanent members (China, France, Russia, the UK and the US). The Assembly then needs a two-thirds majority of those present and voting. So 129 yes votes out of 193, if all vote, and no veto from a permanent member. South Sudan was the last to join, in 2011. Palestine and the Holy See sit as non-member observers.
figure: 193 members; 9 of 15 in Council with 0 vetoes; 2/3 in Assembly (129 if all 193 vote)

sources.t: UN Charter, Chapter II
UN Charter, Chapter IV
UN Charter, Chapter V
UN: Growth in United Nations membership
UN: Non-Member States

need: Know how small a real State can be
what: Size is no bar. Small States counted by the World Bank in 2024 include Tuvalu at 9,646 people, Nauru at 11,947 and Palau at 17,695. All three hold natural land and have recognition from others. So a new project's obstacle lies in territory and consent, since a population of about 10,000 is already enough for a UN seat in practice. San Marino, Monaco and Liechtenstein have 34,000 to 40,000 people.

sources.t: World Bank API: population (SP.POP.TOTL), 2024

what: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties applies to agreements between States, and Article 6 says every State can conclude them. An unrecognized entity's 'treaty' is, for other countries, a private document. That matters because nearly everything else on this list runs on treaties: extradition, air services, postal, tax and ITU membership. The Court's 2010 Kosovo opinion concerns only whether a declaration broke the law.
figure: Art. 6: every State has capacity to conclude treaties

sources.t: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969
ICJ, Kosovo advisory opinion 2010, full text (lagen.nu copy)

what: ISO 3166 is the international list of two- and three-letter country codes, used by banks, shipping, airlines, web domains and passports. As reported on Wikipedia from the standard's Maintenance Agency, the only way in is to be registered in either the UN Terminology Bulletin Country Names or the UN Statistics Division's Standard Country or Area Codes. So the door runs through the UN. Kosovo uses XK, a code from the 'user-assigned' range, outside the official list. ISO's own page refused automated access, so this rests on a secondary source.

sources.t: Wikipedia: ISO 3166-1 (criteria for inclusion, citing the ISO 3166 Maintenance Agency)
Wikipedia: XK (user assigned code)

what: Country domains such as .fr are tied to ISO 3166. RFC 1591, the 1994 document that set the policy, says IANA 'is not in the business of deciding what is and what is not a country', and that the ISO list was picked because ISO has a procedure for that decision. So a new '.xx' follows only after a place gets its ISO code. Anyone can still buy an ordinary .com or a domain under another country's code, which means your web identity sits under another registry's rules.

sources.t: RFC 1591: Domain Name System Structure and Delegation
IANA: Root Zone Database

what: Blocks of IP addresses come from regional registries. ARIN, the North American one, says businesses, nonprofits or government entities are eligible, including individuals who meet the legal requirements of the jurisdiction where they conduct business. So a registered legal entity in a real jurisdiction is the normal route. A self-declared State could only apply through a company elsewhere, or rely on an upstream provider. Either way, the provider's home country can cut service.

sources.t: ARIN: Requesting number resources

what: ISO 4217 assigns codes such as USD and EUR. SIX, the Swiss exchange group, is the official Maintenance Agency and calls itself the only recognized, authoritative source on currency code designations. Codes matter because banks and trading systems use them to book payments. Without one, a currency cannot be listed on normal payment rails, which limits it to local paper or to a private token. We could read SIX's page and amendment notices, but could not retrieve ISO's own page describing who may apply.

sources.t: SIX: Data standards, Maintenance Agency for ISO 4217

need: Choose: own money, someone else's, or crypto
what: Printing notes costs little, and Minerva, Sealand and New Utopia all produced a currency or pictures of one. Legal tender status means courts in your place accept it to settle debts, which helps only where you have courts others respect. Outsiders will take your money only if they can swap it for something. Crypto looks like a way around this, yet the businesses that convert crypto to dollars are regulated in their home countries. Your people therefore end up subject to those countries' rules at the point of exchange.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Republic of Minerva
Wikipedia: Principality of Sealand
Deseret News: SEC says New Utopia offer is just another web scam (1999)
Mayer Brown: FATF revises AML standards for certain funds transfers (Aug 2025)

what: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) writes the standard that most countries' anti-money-laundering rules follow. Recommendation 16, the Travel Rule, requires financial institutions and virtual asset service providers to share who sent and who receives a transfer. For cross-border transfers above USD/EUR 1,000, the 2025 revision requires the beneficiary's name, account number and country and town. The revisions take effect at the end of 2030 and reach crypto firms indirectly. FATF's Recommendation 15 on new technologies is the route for crypto firms. FATF's own site blocked retrieval, so this comes from a law firm's summary and Elliptic.

sources.t: Mayer Brown: FATF revises AML standards for certain funds transfers (Aug 2025)
Elliptic: What is the Travel Rule?

what: The EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) sets uniform rules for crypto-assets not already covered by financial law, including asset-referenced and e-money tokens (types of stablecoin). It requires white papers and authorization for service providers. Firms already operating before 30 December 2024 could continue only until 1 July 2026 or until a decision on their licence. So any citizen token sold to people in the EU now meets the rules. A project may not be based in the EU, but its customers and exchanges are.
figure: 1 July 2026: last date for the transition

sources.t: ESMA: Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation

what: The US GENIUS Act of 2025 (Public Law 119-27) says US stablecoin issuers need approval from a state or federal regulator and must hold at least one dollar of permitted reserves for each dollar issued. Issuers above $50 billion must file audited statements. Exchanges in the US may offer foreign stablecoins only under set conditions, and Treasury may arrange 'reciprocal' deals with places that have comparable rules. An unrecognized place has no regulator for Treasury to deal with (our reading). The OCC has issued final rules, and Treasury proposed more in 2026.
figure: $1 reserve per $1 issued; audited statements above $50 billion

sources.t: Congressional Research Service IN12553: Overview of the GENIUS Act (Aug 2026)
OCC: GENIUS Act
Jones Day: US Treasury proposes GENIUS Act rules (Aug 2026)

need: Get a bank to bank you
what: International payments travel between banks that hold accounts with each other, called correspondent banks. A new place with no banking law or supervisor gives them no one to rely on. The Financial Stability Board reports a steady fall in those relationships: active correspondents dropped 3.4% in 2018, 4.1% in 2017 and 3.9% in 2016, with US dollar links falling fastest and smaller, higher-risk places hit hardest. This retreat is called de-risking. Without a correspondent, your people cannot receive a wire. Newer data was not retrieved.

sources.t: FSB: Correspondent Banking Data Report (2017)
FSB: Correspondent banking data, May 2019
BIS CPMI: Correspondent banking, consultative report

what: SWIFT is the messaging network banks use to instruct payments. Regional law binds it: in March 2022 an EU regulation banned the service for seven Russian banks. SWIFT's own eligibility pages refused automated access, so we cannot quote its criteria here. The practical path for a new place is a licensed bank, which needs a licensing authority other countries accept. Crypto rails avoid SWIFT, and they then run into the exchange and stablecoin rules above.

sources.t: Kelley Drye: EU removes 7 Russian banks from SWIFT (2022)

what: FATF lists places with weak anti-money-laundering rules. An IMF paper by Kida and Paetzold estimates that grey-listing cuts capital inflows by about 7.6% of GDP. After the June 2026 meeting, 22 places were on the list, and an industry summary reports four removals in October 2026 (Bulgaria, Monaco, Côte d'Ivoire and DR Congo), which would leave 18 if none were added. Iran, North Korea and Myanmar sit on the separate high-risk list. A place FATF has never assessed would have no clean record to show banks (our reading).

sources.t: Kida and Paetzold, The Impact of Gray-Listing on Capital Flows, IMF WP/21/153
New Zealand DIA: Jurisdictions under increased monitoring, June 2026
AML UAE: FATF grey list update, 19 June 2026
Citadel365: FATF update October 2026

need: Issue a passport other countries accept
what: ICAO Doc 9303 sets the passport format. Part 3 says the issuing-State codes come from the ISO 3166 agency, plus separate lists for bodies such as the UN and INTERPOL. So recognized passports link back to the UN lists above. ICAO has 193 member States, and joining under the Chicago Convention means being a UN member, or winning four-fifths of ICAO's Assembly with UN approval (Art. 92-93). Printing a booklet in this format still gets no code on these lists, so machine readers and border systems have no entry for it (our reading).
figure: 193 ICAO members; 4/5 vote for non-UN States

sources.t: ICAO Doc 9303 Part 3, Specifications Common to all MRTDs
ICAO: Member States
Chicago Convention 1944, text (McGill Institute of Air and Space Law)

need: Stay clear of fantasy and camouflage passports
what: A camouflage passport looks real but names a non-existent country or entity. A fantasy passport is a similar novelty, not valid for travel. Sealand's passports were called fantasy passports by the Council of the EU, per Wikipedia. In 1997 the Bates family revoked them after finding an international money-laundering ring using them. In US law it is a crime to falsely make 'any passport or instrument purporting to be a passport' intended for use, and to use one (18 USC 1543). Using one at a border may bring charges under such laws (our reading). The EU glossary itself could not be retrieved.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Camouflage passport
Wikipedia: Principality of Sealand
18 U.S. Code 1543: Forgery or false use of passport

need: Know that new citizenship leaves US tax in place
what: The US taxes its citizens on worldwide income wherever they live. The Supreme Court upheld this in Cook v. Tait (1924), for a citizen living in Mexico with Mexican income. The duty follows citizenship, so joining a micronation changes nothing (our reading). Americans abroad must still file. Anyone hoping to live on a platform tax-free therefore faces a return every year until they formally give up US nationality. The State Department's page on statelessness could not be retrieved, so that risk is not detailed here.

sources.t: IRS: US citizens and resident aliens abroad
Cook v. Tait, 265 U.S. 47 (1924)

need: Renounce and pay the exit bill
what: Giving up US citizenship formally costs a government fee. The fee was $2,350 from 2015 until a final rule published in March 2026 cut it to $450, so the $2,350 figure often quoted is out of date. Separately, 'covered expatriates' pay an exit tax. That means anyone with $2 million or more in net worth, or average income tax above $206,000 a year (2025 figure), or who has not certified five years of compliance. They are treated as selling all assets the day before leaving, after an exclusion of $890,000 for 2025.
figure: $450 fee since March 2026 (was $2,350); $2 million net-worth test

sources.t: PBS NewsHour: State Department slashes fee for renouncing US citizenship by 80% to $450
22 CFR 22.1: Schedule of fees for consular services
IRS: Expatriation tax

what: Foreign banks report US account holders to the IRS under FATCA, the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act. Americans must also report foreign financial assets above set limits. Many other countries swap account data under the OECD's Common Reporting Standard. A report on the Global Forum gives 171 million accounts worth nearly EUR 13 trillion, 172 member jurisdictions, and about EUR 135 billion in extra revenue. So your bank tells your home tax office you have the account, whichever flag you live under. This figure comes from a news summary because the OECD's report page returned no such numbers.

sources.t: IRS: Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act
RegFollower: OECD Global Forum reports progress on tax transparency

need: Fly a real flag or be boardable
what: On the high seas, a ship needs a State's flag, with a 'genuine link' to that State (UNCLOS Art. 91). Warships may board on suspicion of no nationality (Art. 110(1)(d)). A ship using several flags may be treated as having none (Art. 92(2)). In US drug law, a 'vessel without nationality' includes one whose claimed registry is denied by the nation named, or whose master makes no claim when asked (46 USC 70502). A real flag means living under that State's law and duties on safety and crew (Art. 94). Choosing a landlocked flag is allowed (Art. 90), since any State may run a register.

sources.t: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, full text
46 U.S. Code 70502: Maritime Drug Law Enforcement Act definitions

need: Avoid piracy, broadcasting and slave-trade powers
what: Three acts open a ship to foreign warships regardless of flag. Piracy: any State may seize a pirate ship and try those aboard (Art. 105), and piracy covers violence or detention for private ends against another ship or in a place outside any State's jurisdiction (Art. 101). Slave trade: suspicion allows a visit (Art. 110) and a slave who reaches any ship is free (Art. 99). Unauthorized broadcasting: any State receiving the signal or suffering interference may arrest the person and seize the equipment (Art. 109). A pirate-radio-style funding model therefore invites arrest.
figure: 5 kinds of State can prosecute unauthorized broadcasts

sources.t: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, full text

need: Decide who prosecutes crime on your platform
what: With no recognized court, the answer is any State with a link. The flag or registry State applies its law. A person's own State often does too: US law reaches 'any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation' for offenses by or against a US national (18 USC 7(7)). Other States may act on piracy or broadcasting. Your own court's verdict would not be accepted by others as binding, and locking someone up on your platform could itself count as detention for private ends under Art. 101, or as kidnapping under the home State's law (our reading).

sources.t: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, full text
18 U.S. Code 7: Special maritime and territorial jurisdiction

what: Extradition runs on treaties between governments. In US law, the judge's power starts with 'a treaty or convention for extradition' with a foreign government (18 USC 3184). A place with no treaties cannot ask for anyone back. Countries where your citizens travel can still hand them over to third countries under their own treaties. So a fugitive from one State gains little from a flag, and your residents can be arrested as soon as they land in a port. Thailand's 2019 case shows how a floating home can become a capital charge within days.

sources.t: 18 U.S. Code 3184: Fugitives from foreign country to United States
VOA: Thailand says US man's seasteading home violates sovereignty (2019)

need: Defend it, or know the record
what: Article 2(4) of the UN Charter bars force in Members' international relations against 'any state', which offers an unrecognized entity little cover. Italy took Rose Island 55 days after its declaration and bombed it. Tonga claimed Minerva Reefs within weeks and removed later occupiers with troops. Thailand raided a seastead in 2019 and raised the death penalty. Croatia has jailed and fined Liberland visitors. Sealand survived a 1978 armed takeover by hired mercenaries, and Britain later placed it within its waters by law. In Antarctica and on the Moon, military bases are barred by treaty for parties.

need: Plan for medical care and rescue
what: Masters must rescue people in danger at sea (UNCLOS Art. 98), so a nearby ship should come, and coastal States run search-and-rescue services for their waters. After rescue you land in someone else's country, under their law. In space, parties must rescue and return astronauts and spacecraft staff, and return them to the launching authority (Rescue Agreement Art. 2, 4; Outer Space Treaty Art. V). That return runs to a State, so a self-declared one has no standing. A hospital of your own is a cost in the budget, and specialist care means going ashore.

sources.t: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, full text
Rescue Agreement, text (UNOOSA)
Outer Space Treaty, text (UNOOSA)

what: OFAC, the US sanctions office, binds all US citizens and permanent residents wherever they are located, plus US entities and their foreign branches. Blocked people's property must be frozen. EU sanctions cut seven Russian banks from SWIFT in 2022, and the rule extended to entities they own by 50% or more. So any US person who helps a listed person at your project takes on personal exposure, wherever the project sits (our reading). OFAC publishes civil penalty tables each year.

sources.t: OFAC FAQ: Who must comply with OFAC sanctions
OFAC: Basic information on OFAC and sanctions (FAQs)
Kelley Drye: EU removes 7 Russian banks from SWIFT (2022)

need: Avoid securities fraud when selling land or bonds
what: Selling a stake in a future country to the public can count as selling securities. In 1999 the SEC sued Lazarus Long, born Howard Turney, over a $350 million bond offering at 9.5% for 'New Utopia', a Caribbean nation that had not been built. The court froze the funds, and in January 2000 he consented to a permanent injunction. He had raised $24,000, and the disgorgement order was waived because he could not pay. The charges were under Securities Act Sections 5 and 17(a) and Exchange Act Section 10(b). Citizenship tokens with a promised return carry the same risk.

sources.t: SEC Litigation Release 16425: Lazarus R. Long (Feb 2000)
Deseret News: SEC says New Utopia offer is just another web scam (1999)

need: Understand what a lunar deed is worth
what: Dennis Hope's Lunar Embassy has sold acres since 1980. Discover reported 4.25 million buyers and over $9 million in sales at $19.99, and National Geographic reported 2.5 million plots at $22.49. The Outer Space Treaty bars national appropriation, and the Moon Agreement bars private property in the surface for its parties. The International Institute of Space Law issued a statement warning that such deeds could mislead individuals. This research found no court or government registry backing them. Buyers receive a printed deed.

sources.t: Discover: The Man Who Sells the Moon
National Geographic: Who owns the Moon?
International Institute of Space Law: Statement on claims to property rights regarding the Moon and other celestial bodies
Outer Space Treaty, text (UNOOSA)
Moon Agreement, text (UNOOSA)

what: A US launch needs an FAA licence, as does any launch by a US citizen outside the US (51 USC 50904). Licence rules sit in 14 CFR Part 450. The licensee must carry third-party insurance sized to the 'maximum probable loss', capped at $500 million or the most available on the world market at a reasonable cost (51 USC 50914; 14 CFR 440.9). The payload must also comply with US law, and the government can block a launch on safety, national security or foreign policy grounds. So a US launch brings its supervision with it.

sources.t: 51 U.S. Code 50904: Restrictions on launches, operations and reentries
51 U.S. Code 50914: Liability insurance and financial responsibility
14 CFR 440.9: Insurance requirements for licensed or permitted activities
14 CFR Part 450: Launch and reentry license requirements

need: Register your object with a State
what: The Registration Convention requires a launching State to register each object and give the UN its orbit and purpose (Arts. II, IV). The registering State then keeps jurisdiction and control over the object and anyone aboard (Outer Space Treaty Art. VIII). That is the central block for any orbital nation: only States run these registries, and if you are on one you are under that State. The Convention has 77 parties. Private people cannot register themselves.

sources.t: Registration Convention, text (UNOOSA)
UNOOSA A/AC.105/C.2/2026/CRP.9: Status of International Agreements as at 1 January 2026
Outer Space Treaty, text (UNOOSA)

need: Pay for damage from your spacecraft
what: A launching State is liable for damage its space object causes on Earth or to aircraft, with no need to prove fault (Liability Convention Art. II). In space, liability depends on fault (Art. III). States that launch together share the liability (Art. V). A launching State includes one that launches, procures the launch, or whose territory is used (Art. I). The Convention has 100 parties. Any State exposed in this way will demand licensing and insurance before it lets you near a pad.

sources.t: Liability Convention, text (UNOOSA)
UNOOSA A/AC.105/C.2/2026/CRP.9: Status of International Agreements as at 1 January 2026

need: Get radio spectrum through a member State
what: Spacecraft and many ships need radio frequencies, which are coordinated by the ITU. Its Constitution treats frequencies and orbits as limited natural resources (Art. 44) and bars harmful interference (Art. 45). Frequency assignment notices are submitted by national administrations and recorded in the Master International Frequency Register. ITU has 194 member States. Non-UN States can apply only with the agreement of two-thirds of members under Art. 2(c) A self-declared State therefore needs a member to file for it, which puts that member's regulator in charge.

sources.t: ITU Constitution
ITU: Membership
ITU Radiocommunication Bureau: Space Services Department

need: Win flight rights and landing rights
what: Scheduled international air service needs special permission from each State flown over or landed in (Chicago Art. 6). Non-scheduled flights have more freedom, but only among contracting States' aircraft (Art. 5). Every aircraft has one State of registry and must bear its marks (Arts. 17-20). So an airline from an unrecognized place cannot use these rights, since it has no contracting State behind it. The workaround is to rely on another country's registered aircraft. Pilotless craft need separate authorization (Art. 8).

sources.t: Chicago Convention 1944, text (McGill Institute of Air and Space Law)

what: Each place has its own process. BBNJ Art. 28 requires impact assessment by parties for planned activities in areas beyond national jurisdiction, since January 2026. Antarctica requires prior assessment under Madrid Protocol Art. 8, and Art. 7 bans mining. At sea, the London Protocol treats dumping as forbidden unless permitted. Space parties must avoid harmful contamination (Art. IX), and COSPAR sets planetary protection rules. The South China Sea tribunal held that reclamation at seven reefs breached a State's duties on the marine environment. If your home State is a party, it applies these rules to you.

what: No project in the sources has produced its own food at scale. A person needs about 0.84 kg of oxygen a day (NASA), and food use on the ISS ran at 2.77 kg per crew member per day. The ISS has reached 98% water recovery, and it still relies on deliveries for tanks, water bags and food. At sea, a platform needs a port. Oceanix's Busan design plans to make its own energy on site, though that remains a plan. Dependence on a neighbor's port gives that neighbor control, as Italy's blockade of Rose Island showed.
figure: 0.84 kg oxygen and 2.77 kg food per person per day

what: Montevideo asks for a permanent population without giving a number. Tuvalu has 9,646 people. Salotti's Scientific Reports model puts the minimum for a self-sustaining Mars colony at 110, based on labor time, under strong assumptions. Rule of thumb from these cases: a society can be small on paper, and a working one needs doctors, engineers, teachers and courts. Sealand shows the limit: Wikipedia reports one permanent resident as of August 2024, and Minnesota JLST reported two in 2019.

what: Published figures are all estimates for things not yet built. Oceanix Busan: $200 million stated in 2021, or $627 million at the developers' $10,000 per square metre, for 15.5 acres and 12,000 people. Freedom Ship: as high as about $16 billion for 80,000 people, stalled for decades. Pangeos: about $8 billion for 60,000. A law journal puts even a small deep-sea platform for a few residents at $50 million. On those numbers, cost per resident runs from about $17,000 to $200,000 for the larger plans, and far more for a small platform (our arithmetic).

what: NASA's Jones calculated $54,500 per kg for the Space Shuttle to low orbit, and $2,720 per kg for Falcon 9 at its 2018 price of $62 million. By early 2026 a dedicated Falcon 9 was about $74 million, or $3,246 per kg at full capacity. Rideshare starts at $350,000 for 50 kg. Voyager's filings imply $90 million for a Starship flight, once certified, by Motley Fool's reading. Those are rocket costs alone. Food alone, at 2.77 kg a day, comes to about 1,000 kg a person each year, or about $3.3 million at the Falcon 9 rate (our arithmetic).

Vast has committed more than $1 billion to its single-module Haven-1, which has slipped to no earlier than the first quarter of 2027, and sold no crew seat as of that report. Axiom gave a price of $55 million a seat for a 10-day trip to the ISS, plus NASA charges reported then as $2,000 per person per day for food and more for support.

what: The record from these sources is mostly online sign-ups and small purchases. Lunar deed buyers number in the millions at about $20 each. Liberland reported hundreds of thousands of applications. Asgardia reported more than 290,000 citizens in 2019 and over 500,000 sign-ups within three weeks. New Utopia raised $24,000 against a $350 million offer. Próspera drew foreign investors, and its claim against Honduras has fallen from $10.775 billion to $1.63 billion. Real second citizenship has a market too, as with St Kitts and Nevis's programme, running since 1984.
